> [!TLDR]
> Choosing one vacuum hides a continuous symmetry and gives a massive radial mode and a massless Goldstone mode.

<!-- PDF page 370; printed page 362 -->

The example we have just considered illustrates another phenomenon of importance: *spontaneous symmetry-breaking*. The original Lagrangian (11.108) is *even* in $\signal{\phi}$: It is invariant as $\signal{\phi}\to-\signal{\phi}$. But the reformulated Lagrangian (11.113) is *not* even in $\signal{\eta}$; the symmetry has been “broken.” How did this happen? It happened because the “vacuum” (whichever of the two ground states we care to work with) does not share the symmetry of the Lagrangian. (The collection of *all* ground states, of course, *does*, but to set up the Feynman formalism we are obliged to work with one or the other of them, and that spoils the symmetry.) We call this “spontaneous” symmetry-breaking because no *external* agency is responsible (as, for example, gravity breaks the three-dimensional symmetry in this room, making “up” and “down” quite different from “left” and “right”). To put it the other way around, the true symmetry of the system is “hidden” by the arbitrary selection of a particular (asymmetrical) ground state. There are examples of spontaneous symmetry-breaking in many branches of physics. Take,

<!-- PDF page 371; printed page 363 -->

![[elementary-particles-qed-figure-11-2-plastic-strip.svg|**Fig. 11.2** Spontaneous symmetry-breaking in a plastic strip.]]

for instance, a thin plastic strip (say, a short ruler). If you squeeze the ends together, it will snap into a curved configuration, but it can just as well buckle to the left as to the right—both are ground states for the system, and either one breaks the left-right symmetry (see Fig. 11.2).

But the spontaneously broken symmetry we have just considered was a *discrete* symmetry, with just two ground states. More interesting things happen when we consider *continuous* symmetries. (Replace the plastic strip in Figure 11.2 with a plastic *rod*—say, a knitting needle. Then it can buckle in *any* direction, not just left or right.[^ep-11-8-ferromagnet]) It is easy to construct a Lagrangian with spontaneously broken continuous symmetry. For example

$$
\energy{\mathcal L}
=\tfrac12(\partial_\mu\signal{\phi_1})(\partial^\mu\signal{\phi_1})
+\tfrac12(\partial_\mu\signal{\phi_2})(\partial^\mu\signal{\phi_2})
+\tfrac12\mechanical{\mu}^2(\signal{\phi_1}^2+\signal{\phi_2}^2)
-\tfrac14\lambda^2(\signal{\phi_1}^2+\signal{\phi_2}^2)^2
\tag{11.115}
$$

This is identical to equation (11.108), except that now there are *two* fields, $\signal{\phi_1}$ and $\signal{\phi_2}$, and because $\energy{\mathcal L}$ involves only the sum of the squares, it is invariant under *rotations* in $\signal{\phi_1}$, $\signal{\phi_2}$ space.[^ep-11-8-rotation]

This time the “potential energy” function is

$$
\energy{\mathcal U}
=-\tfrac12\mechanical{\mu}^2(\signal{\phi_1}^2+\signal{\phi_2}^2)
+\tfrac14\lambda^2(\signal{\phi_1}^2+\signal{\phi_2}^2)^2
\tag{11.116}
$$

and the minima lie on a circle of radius $\mechanical{\mu}/\lambda$:

$$
\signal{\phi_{1\min}}^2+\signal{\phi_{2\min}}^2=\mechanical{\mu}^2/\lambda^2
\tag{11.117}
$$

(see Fig. 11.3). To apply the Feynman calculus, we have to expand about a *particular* ground state (“the vacuum”)—we may as well pick

$$
\signal{\phi_{1\min}}=\mechanical{\mu}/\lambda;\qquad \signal{\phi_{2\min}}=0
\tag{11.118}
$$

As before, we introduce new fields, $\signal{\eta}$ and $\signal{\xi}$, which are the fluctuations about this vacuum state:

$$
\signal{\eta}\equiv\signal{\phi_1}-\mechanical{\mu}/\lambda;\qquad
\signal{\xi}\equiv\signal{\phi_2}
\tag{11.119}
$$

[^ep-11-8-ferromagnet]: A more sophisticated example is the ferromagnet: In the ground state all the electron spins are aligned, but the *direction* of alignment is an accident of history. The *theory* is symmetrical, but a given piece of iron has to pick a particular orientation, and that breaks the symmetry.

[^ep-11-8-rotation]: Group theoretically, it is invariant under $SO(2)$: $\signal{\phi_1}\to\signal{\phi_1}\cos\mechanical{\theta}+\signal{\phi_2}\sin\mechanical{\theta}$, $\signal{\phi_2}\to-\signal{\phi_1}\sin\mechanical{\theta}+\signal{\phi_2}\cos\mechanical{\theta}$, for any “rotation angle” $\mechanical{\theta}$. (See Problem 4.6.)

**Fig. 11.3** The potential function (11.116). The graph can rotate.

Rewriting the Lagrangian in terms of these new field variables, we find (Problem 11.22):

$$
\begin{aligned}
\energy{\mathcal L}
&=\left[\frac12(\partial_\mu\signal{\eta})(\partial^\mu\signal{\eta})
-\mechanical{\mu}^2\signal{\eta}^2\right]
+\left[\frac12(\partial_\mu\signal{\xi})(\partial^\mu\signal{\xi})\right]\\
&\quad+\left[\mechanical{\mu}\lambda(\signal{\eta}^3+\signal{\eta}\signal{\xi}^2)
-\frac{\lambda^2}{4}(\signal{\eta}^4+\signal{\xi}^4+2\signal{\eta}^2\signal{\xi}^2)\right]
+\mechanical{\mu}^4/(4\lambda^2)
\end{aligned}
\tag{11.120}
$$

The first term is a free Klein–Gordon Lagrangian (11.11) for the field $\signal{\eta}$, which evidently carries a mass

$$
\mechanical{m_\eta}=\sqrt2\mechanical{\mu}\energy{\hbar}/\mechanical{c}
\tag{11.121}
$$

[the same as before, see eq. (11.114)]; the second term is a free Lagrangian for the field $\signal{\xi}$, which is *massless*:

$$
\mechanical{m_\xi}=0
\tag{11.122}
$$

and the third term defines five couplings:

![[elementary-particles-qed-chapter11-goldstone-scalar-vertices.svg|The five scalar couplings involve three eta fields, one eta and two xi fields, four eta fields, four xi fields, and two fields of each type.]]

(the final constant, of course, is irrelevant). In this form the Lagrangian doesn't look symmetrical at all; the symmetry of (11.115) has been broken (or rather, “hidden”) by the selection of a particular vacuum state.

The important thing to notice here is that one of the fields $(\signal{\xi})$ is *automatically massless*. This is no accident. It can be shown (Goldstone's theorem<sup>10</sup>) that spontaneous breaking of a *continuous* global symmetry is *always* accompanied by the appearance of one or more massless scalar (spin-0) particles (we call them “Goldstone bosons”).[^ep-11-8-restoring] Well, this is a disaster; we were hoping to use

[^ep-11-8-restoring]: Intuitively, this is related to the fact that there is no resistance to excitations in the $\signal{\xi}$ direction. Flick the bent knitting needle and it will spin freely about the axis, whereas radial excitations encounter a restoring force, and the system oscillates.

<!-- PDF page 373; printed page 365 -->

the mechanism of spontaneous symmetry-breaking to account for the mass of the weak interaction gauge fields, but now we find that this introduces a massless scalar boson, and there is no such thing on the roster of known elementary particles.[^ep-11-8-detection] But hold on, for there is one final incredible twist in the story. It comes when we apply the idea of spontaneous symmetry-breaking to the case of *local* gauge invariance.

[^ep-11-8-detection]: It is hard to imagine that such a particle could have escaped detection. With *heavy* particles this is always a possibility—maybe you just didn't have enough energy to *produce* it—but a *massless* particle would surely have shown up somewhere, if only in the form of “missing” energy and momentum.

## Physical quantities

| Symbol | Unit | Quantity | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\energy{\mathcal L},\energy{\mathcal U}$ | $\unit{erg/cm^3}$ | Lagrangian and potential densities | The field function and its circle of degenerate minima. |
| $\signal{\phi},\signal{\phi_1},\signal{\phi_2},\signal{\eta},\signal{\xi}$ | $\unit{g^{1/2}\,cm^{1/2}/s}$ | Scalar fields | Original fields and fluctuations about the chosen vacuum. |
| $\signal{\phi_{1\min}},\signal{\phi_{2\min}}$ | $\unit{g^{1/2}\,cm^{1/2}/s}$ | Vacuum field values | Coordinates of the chosen potential minimum. |
| $\mechanical{\mu}$ | $\unit{cm^{-1}}$ | Mass parameter | Sets the radial excitation's mass scale. |
| $\lambda$ | $\unit{s/(g^{1/2}\,cm^{3/2})}$ | Scalar coupling | Sets the quartic interaction and vacuum radius. |
| $\mechanical{m_\eta},\mechanical{m_\xi}$ | $\unit{g}$ | Scalar particle masses | Massive radial mode and massless Goldstone mode. |
| $\mechanical{\theta}$ | $\unit{rad}$ | Internal rotation angle | Rotates the two scalar fields into one another. |
| $\energy{\hbar}$ | $\unit{erg\,s}$ | Reduced Planck constant | Converts the radial mass parameter to particle mass. |
| $\mechanical{c}$ | $\unit{cm/s}$ | Speed of light | Relates the mass parameter to particle mass. |
